name: Kafa
confidence_why: Reinisch 1888 and Cerulli 1951 (as summarized by Cohen 1988) both put the Kafa accent on the heaviest of the last three syllables and differ only in how weight is counted, but Cohen 1988 himself warns that closer study may revise this, and the more recent first-hand descriptions, Taddese 2001, Theil 2007 and Theil 2023, treat Kafa as a tone language, leaving open whether this weight-based accent is stress or tone.
catalog_citation: Reinisch, Leo. 1888. Die Kafa-Sprache in Nordost-Afrika. I. Sitzungsberichte der kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien, philosophisch-historische Classe 116: 53-143 (Separatabdruck, Wien: F. Tempsky). Lautlehre, 3) 'Der Accent', §31.
catalog_locator: Separatum pp. 37-39 (= Sitzungsberichte [87]-[89]) of archive.org item diekafasprachein00rein; separatum pages 37-39 read.
catalog_quote: 31) Hinsichtlich des Accentes ist für das Kafa als Hauptregel anzusehen, dass der Ton nur auf einer der drei letzten Wortsilben, und zwar hier auf derjenigen ruht, deren Vocal die übrigen an Gehalt überwigt. Der Vocal einer geschlossenen Silbe überwigt hinsichtlich der Betonung den einer offenen, daher hat das Kafa, dessen Wörter fast sämmtlich vocalisch auslauten, den Accent nur in wenigen speziellen Fällen auf der letzten, sonst stets auf der vorletzten oder drittletzten Silbe des Wortes. ... c) Bei allen zweisilbigen vocalisch auslautenden Wörtern ruht der Accent auf der vorletzten Silbe, gleichgiltig ob der Vocal derselben kurz oder lang ist, als: níhō Vater, índē Mutter ... d) Bei den drei- und mersilbigen Wörtern ruht der Accent auf der vorletzten Silbe, wenn deren Vocal an Gewicht den der drittletzten übertrifft, z. B. baqérō Saubone, aríngō Peitsche ...; auch wenn die Vocale der vorletzten und drittletzten an Gewicht sich gleichstehen, aber der auslautende Vocal lang ist, wie: kasárō ... Kole, qacámō Hyäne ... e) Auf der drittletzten Silbe ruht der Accent: α) wenn der Vocal der letzten Silbe kurz ist, wie: wáqwaqe prügeln, aber waqwáqō Prügelei ... β) Lautet die Silbe auf einen langen Vocal aus, so steht der Accent nur dann auf der drittletzten, wenn der Vocal der vorletzten Silbe dem der drittletzten an Gewicht nachsteht, wie: engángilō ... Eidechse, ómborō Reis, bárbarō Pfeffer

new_statements.translation: 31) As regards accent, the main rule for Kafa is that the tone rests only on one of the last three syllables of the word, namely on the one whose vowel outweighs the others in content. The vowel of a closed syllable outweighs that of an open one with respect to accentuation; hence Kafa, whose words almost all end in a vowel, has the accent on the final syllable only in a few special cases, otherwise always on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable of the word. ... c) In all disyllabic vowel-final words the accent rests on the penult ... d) In tri- and polysyllabic words the accent rests on the penult if its vowel exceeds that of the antepenult in weight

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Reinisch 1888: accent confined to a final three-syllable window and assigned by vowel/syllable weight (closed > open; vowel 'weight'; long final vowel favours penult): disyllables = penult; longer words = penult if heavier than antepenult (or equal and final vowel long), otherwise antepenult; final accent only in negative imperatives (hamáy), imperatives of triradical verbs (saqár) and the genitive in -i, explained as enclitics retaining their own tone. Cerulli 1951 (snippet) states the same core pattern (trisyllables: initial/antepenult unless the penult vowel is long). HOWEVER modern primary work (Taddese Habte Addo 1999/2001; Theil 2007, 2023; Azeb Amha 2017) analyses Kafa as a two-tone (H/L) language with the vowel mora as TBU and 'tonal bridge' processes, and treats the earlier 'stress' descriptions as pre-tonal misreadings; Fleming 1976 conversely called tone an epiphenomenon of stress/length. What the modern sources say about stress per se could not be read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Reinisch: none described; only note that suffixed particles keep their own accent (e.g. ážerā gúttā-ná 'twelve').
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in negative imperative (hamáy 'do not go'), positive imperative of triradical verbs (saqár), genitive -í (qēt-í kéllō); loan name Amán with final accent; negative infinitive always penult (hamáye).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms from 19th-century elicitation; Reinisch uses 'Accent'/'Ton'/'Betonung' interchangeably (pre-tonal framework). Modern analyses: lexical/grammatical tone (2 tones), so the catalog entry should be flagged tonal with the 1888 weight-window accent rule recorded as the historical stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Reinisch 1888 describes 'Kafa' from speakers interviewed outside Kafa (19th-c. data); it is the same language as modern Kafi Noonoo (kafa1242), not Shekkacho/Moča (moy). Note Glottolog 5.1 mis-tags Theil 2007 'Kafa phonology' to Shekkacho [moy] by autotranslation; it is about Kafa [kbr]. Theil 2023 distinguishes E-dialects and A-dialects of Kafa; his morphology is based on A-dialects.

new_statements.quote: 2.4. Tons et accent. Les documents publiés sur la variété de kafa considérée ici ne soulignent pas la présence de tons. Cependant en motcha, parler appartenant au même groupe, on a mis en relief l'existence d'un système de trois tonèmes [...]. On peut résumer de la manière suivante les indications fournies pour l'accent. Celui-ci porterait essentiellement sur la syllabe contenant la troisième more à partir de la fin du mot, toute syllabe en CV étant comptée pour une more et toute syllabe en CV: ou CVC pour deux mores. Des exceptions sont constituées par quelques suffixes, les uns portant toujours et les autres ne portant jamais l'accent.
new_statements.translation: 2.4. Tones and accent. The published documents on the variety of Kafa considered here do not note the presence of tones. However in Mocha, a variety belonging to the same group, a system of three tonemes has been brought out [...]. The indications given for the accent can be summarized as follows. It would fall essentially on the syllable containing the third mora from the end of the word, every CV syllable counting as one mora and every CV: or CVC syllable as two morae. Exceptions are constituted by a few suffixes, some always bearing the accent and others never bearing it.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kafa has an empty rule; the only existing statement is Reinisch 1888 (accent on one of the last three syllables, the one whose vowel outweighs the others, closed syllable outweighing open). Cohen, summarizing Cerulli 1951, gives the same weight-sensitive placement in a precise mora-counting form (third mora from the end, CV = 1, CVV/CVC = 2) and adds the suffix exceptions. The two formulations agree on Reinisch's examples of types CV.CV(:), CV.CV.CV: and CVC.CV.CV, but for a few of Reinisch's antepenult examples with a heavy antepenult and a final long vowel (engángilō, ómborō) the mora rule as stated would put the accent on the penult; this may reflect differences in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the syllable that contains the third mora counted from the end of the word; CV syllables count one mora, CVV and CVC syllables two. So a final long vowel or closed final syllable pulls the accent to the penult, and a light final syllable leaves it on the antepenult (a mora-counting window over the last three syllables). No tones are reported for Kafa proper in the sources used (Cerulli 1951, Leslau 1959), though Cohen notes that Mocha, of the same group, has three tonemes and that a dedicated survey might change the picture for Kafa.
new_statements.exceptions: A few suffixes are exceptions: some always carry the accent, others never do. Cohen also flags that the tonal status of Kafa proper is unsettled ('Il n'est pas exclu qu'une enquête particulière sur ce point ne modifie les données utilisables aujourd'hui pour le kafa proprement dit').
new_statements.identity_note: Cohen 1988 describes 'la variété de kafa considérée ici', i.e. Kafa proper as documented by Cerulli 1951 and Leslau 1959, and explicitly contrasts it with Mocha (motcha, Shekkacho), a separate variety/language of the same Gonga group for which Leslau 1959 reports three tonemes (high, falling, low on long vowels only); Cohen also notes bocha/garo as an extinct variety of Kafa. Reinisch 1888 describes Kafa proper (Kaffa) from his own informant material; no sub-dialect is named in the accent section.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is confined to the last three syllables and goes to the heaviest of them (closed syllable outweighs open; long vowel outweighs short). Sub-rules: (a) final accent only in the negative imperative, the positive imperative of triradical verbs, and the genitive ending -i, plus the loan name Amán; (b) the negative infinitive is always penult-accented; (c) disyllables ending in a vowel are penult-accented whatever the vowel length; (d) in words of three or more syllables the penult is accented when its vowel outweighs the antepenult's, or when they are equal and the final vowel is long; (e) the antepenult is accented when the final vowel is short, or, with a long final vowel, when the penult vowel is lighter than the antepenult's. Enclitic particles keep their own accent when attached (dzerā gúttā-nā 'twelve').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only one accent per word is marked.
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in the negative imperative (hamáj 'do not go'), the positive imperative of triradical verbs (saqár), and the genitive -i (qetí kellō 'the house door', explained as the particle -i keeping its accent); the borrowed name Amán; particles retain their own accent when suffixed; 'Tongesetz' also governs possessive phrases (tā níhō 'my father' vs itōšī nihō 'your (pl.) father').

tone_statements.citation: Teferi Mulugeta & Girma Mengistu. 2023 [Crossref-registered 2022]. The phonology of Kafi Noonoo ideophones. Macrolinguistics and Microlinguistics 4(1): 1-25 (Crossref metadata: 3(1/2): 15-38). doi:10.21744/mami.v3n1/2.29. CC BY 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: According to Taddese (2001) Kafi Noonoo has rising and falling contour tones in addition to the two basic tones: H and L. He states that tone pattern difference in a word brings meaning difference. This shows that tone pattern is another word formation process in the language. Consider the following examples taken from (Taddese, 2001, p. 34). I. Nominals Formed from Other Nouns … 1 a) káʃó 'ripe' b) kàʃò 'soul' c) káʃò 'farm tool' … II. Nominals Formed from Verbs … 4a) gòjó 'to farm' b) gòjò 'farm' … III) Verbs Formed from Verbs 7a) kémó 'to sell' b) kémò 'to buy'
tone_statements.locator: Chapter 5 'Word formation by changing the tone pattern', pp. 74-75; review of Taddese 2001, pp. 10-11; symbols list p. VII
tone_statements.summary: Two basic tones, high and low (after Taddese 2001), with rising and falling contours also occurring; tone alone distinguishes words and derives nouns from verbs and verbs from verbs.

tone_statements.citation: Taddese Habte Addo. 2007. Käfa language. In S. Uhlig (ed.), Encyclopaedia Aethiopica vol. 3 (He-N), 326-327. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
tone_statements.quote: Consonant gemination, vowel length, and tone are phonemic. … In Käfa rising tone (R) appears only on long vowels. … Käfa is basically a register tone language in which a high tone (H) and a low tone (L) are realized on relatively level pitches. E.g.: (1) kášó (H) ‘ripe’ kàšò (L) ‘soul’ kášò (HL) ‘farm tool’ kàšó (LH) ‘breathe’ … Rising and falling contour tones also occur in the language. The falling contour has a very lim ited distribution, being restricted to some morphologically complex forms.
tone_statements.locator: EAE vol. 3 pp. 326-327 (page breaks not shown in the online reproduction), phonology paragraphs of the entry 'Käfa language'
tone_statements.summary: Register tone language with two level tones, high and low, contrasting on words of any vowel length; rising tone only on long vowels, falling contour marginal; tone also has grammatical function.

tone_statements.citation: Taddese Habte Addo. 2001. The Tonology of Kafi Noonoo. (NTNU Working Papers in Linguistics 15.) Trondheim: NTNU [= 1999 MA thesis, 77 pp., hdl 11250/4461120, Cristin 314602, no file deposited].
tone_statements.quote: Taddese (2001:34) identifies two-tone systems in the regular phonology. These are the high (H) and low (L) tones. From the entire data, it is observed that Kafa ideophones uniformly bear high (H) tone except the final vowel. … In ideophones, these terminal vowels carry low tones … Kafa is typologically tone language. The regular phonology of the language uses two lexical tones (the high (H) and low (L) tones) … In contrast to the regular phonology, ideophonic bound stem use the high (H) tone(s) across a word
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.2.4.3 'The role and patterns of tones in Kafa ideophones', p.67; + ch.9 conclusion p.247
tone_statements.summary: Kafa is a tone language with two level lexical tones, high and low (after Taddese 2001); ideophone stems carry high tone throughout, with low tone on nominalizing final vowels.

tone_statements.citation: Fleming, Harold C. 1976. Kefa (Gonga) languages. In M. L. Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia, 351-376 (esp. 366-368). East Lansing: MSU African Studies Center.
tone_statements.quote: Furthermore, Kafi Noonoo is a tone language. The language has high and low tones. [abstract, p. 1] ... Taddese (2001), identifies two-tone systems in the regular phonology. These are the high (H) and low (L) tones. From the entire data, it is observed that Kafi Noonoo ideophones uniformly bear high (H) tone except the final vowel. Like the non-ideophonic words, in ideophones the final vowels are nominalizing suffixes. In ideophones, these terminal vowels carry low tones as in túútè ‘rain-bird’. On the other hand, the high tones in ideophonic words show the intensity of actions or events. [section 8.3, p. 14]
tone_statements.locator: Abstract p. 1; section 8.3 'The roles and patterns of tone in Kafi Noonoo ideophones', p. 14
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, H and L (after Taddese 2001); ideophone stems all-H with a L final nominalizing vowel; no stress statement.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on type: both works opened describe a single weight-sensitive word accent confined to the last three syllables, and neither reports tones for Kafa proper (Cohen 1988 says explicitly that the published documents on this variety do not note tones, while Mocha of the same group has three tonemes). The two formulations differ in detail: Reinisch 1888 ranks syllables by vowel 'weight' (closed > open, long > short) and gives case-by-case sub-rules, whereas Cohen (after Cerulli 1951) states a third-mora-from-the-end rule with CV = 1 and CVV/CVC = 2 morae; applied to a few of Reinisch's antepenult examples with a heavy antepenult and a long final vowel (engángilō, ómborō) the mora rule would predict the penult, which is most plausibly a transcription difference in vowel length between the two descriptions rather than a different rule. Cohen adds suffix exceptions (some suffixes always accented, some never), Reinisch adds final-accent exceptions in imperatives and the genitive -i. A residual tension is with the catalog's label of the Reinisch statement as 'tone language with a stress statement': neither opened work supports a tonal reading

tone.quote: Furthermore, Kafi Noonoo is a tone language. The language has high and low tones. [abstract, p. 1] ... Taddese (2001), identifies two-tone systems in the regular phonology. These are the high (H) and low (L) tones. From the entire data, it is observed that Kafi Noonoo ideophones uniformly bear high (H) tone except the final vowel. Like the non-ideophonic words, in ideophones the final vowels are nominalizing suffixes. In ideophones, these terminal vowels carry low tones as in túútè ‘rain-bird’. On the other hand, the high tones in ideophonic words show the intensity of actions or events. [section 8.3, p. 14]
tone.locator: Abstract p. 1; section 8.3 'The roles and patterns of tone in Kafi Noonoo ideophones', p. 14
tone.summary: Two level tones, H and L (after Taddese 2001); ideophone stems all-H with a L final nominalizing vowel; no stress statement.
tone.says: States that Kafi Noonoo is a tone language with two tones, high and low (regular phonology after Taddese 2001), and gives first-hand tone data on ideophones: ideophonic stems are uniformly H, the final (nominalizing) vowel L (tuute 'rain-bird' H H L); H in ideophones signals intensity. Section 8 lists 'lengthening, tone, intonations and stress' as suprasegmentals but treats only length and tone; no stress rule.

tone.quote: Consonant gemination, vowel length, and tone are phonemic. … In Käfa rising tone (R) appears only on long vowels. … Käfa is basically a register tone language in which a high tone (H) and a low tone (L) are realized on relatively level pitches. E.g.: (1) kášó (H) ‘ripe’ kàšò (L) ‘soul’ kášò (HL) ‘farm tool’ kàšó (LH) ‘breathe’ … Rising and falling contour tones also occur in the language. The falling contour has a very lim ited distribution, being restricted to some morphologically complex forms.
tone.locator: EAE vol. 3 pp. 326-327 (page breaks not shown in the online reproduction), phonology paragraphs of the entry 'Käfa language'
tone.summary: Register tone language with two level tones, high and low, contrasting on words of any vowel length; rising tone only on long vowels, falling contour marginal; tone also has grammatical function.
tone.says: Register tone language with two level tones, high and low, contrasting on words of any vowel length; rising tone only on long vowels, falling contour marginal; tone also has grammatical function.
